content: 1. The numerator represents the number of active health workers who were trained in foreign countries. 2. The denominator is the total number of active health workers, defined by headcounts. 3. Disaggregation is performed by occupation and by both occupation and the country where the training occurred. 4. The indicator measures the percentage of active foreign-trained health workers within the active health workforce. 5. The glossary includes terms such as active health worker, occupation, and foreign-trained health workers. 6. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is annual. 7. Potential data sources include health workforce registries or databases, professional council/chamber/association registers, and health facility data. 8. Further information and related references include publications from OECD (2016), WHO (2015c), and the EU Joint Action on Health Workforce Planning and Forecasting (2016a). 9. The numerator for the indicator percentage of workers in the health and social sector to total civilian workers is the number of persons working in the health or social sector, defined by headcounts. 10. The denominator is the total number of persons employed, also defined by headcounts. 11. Disaggregation is based on health and social sectors as defined by ISIC codes 86 (human health activities), 87 (residential care activities), and 88 (social work activities without accommodation). 12. The indicator calculates the ratio of the number of persons working in health and social sectors to the total number of persons employed in the civilian labor force. 13. The civilian labor force excludes armed forces. 14. People working in health and social sectors include those in ISIC divisions 86, 87, and 88. 15. This indicator aligns with the OECD Health Statistics indicator Total health and social employment. 16. In cases where ISIC activity data are unavailable, the ratio between health employment and total civilian employment can be used as an approximation. 17. The glossary includes terms such as economic activity classification and employment. 18. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is annual. 19. Potential data sources include labor force surveys, tax registries, and insurance or pension fund registries. 20. Further information and related references include publications from the United Nations (2008), WHO (2016c), and OECD (2017a). 21. Module 2 addresses capacity, quality, and gender equality in health workforce education and training. 22. These align with education sector (SDG 4) indicators, which assist in coordinating policies on workforce production. 23. The module also focuses on gender equality and equitable access to education and training. 24. Applications include a master list of accredited health workforce education and training institutions, duration of education and training, applications for education and training, admissions, student-to-educator ratios, exit/drop-out rates, and graduation rates. 25. The indicator existence of a master list of accredited health workforce education and training institutions determines whether such a list is up-to-date and publicly available. 26. The numerator and denominator are not applicable for this indicator. 27. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program. 28. The glossary includes terms such as master list, accreditation, and health workforce education and training institution. 29. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is every three years. 30. Potential data sources include national statistical services, ministries of labor and human resources, ministries of education, and labor bureaus. 31. Further information and related references include UNESCO (2015a) and WHO (2015c). 32. The indicator duration of health workforce education and training measures the number of years required to complete a full curriculum for each health workforce education and training program. 33. The numerator and denominator are not applicable for this indicator. 34. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program. 35. The glossary includes terms such as health workforce education and training program. 36. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is annual. 37. Potential data sources include ministries of education, databases on education and training statistics, and education and training institutions. 38. Further information and related references include WHO (2013e), Pan American Health Organization (2011), and WHO (2015c). 39. The indicator ratio of applications for health workforce education and training to training places is calculated by dividing the number of applications for the first year of a program by the number of training places available for that year. 40. The numerator is the number of applications for education and training places. 41. The denominator is the total number of places available. 42. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program and by sex. 43. The glossary includes terms such as health workforce education and training place and health workforce education and training program. 44. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is annual. 45. Potential data sources include ministries of education, ministries of higher education, and databases on education and training statistics. 46. Further information and related references include WHO (2013e), Pan American Health Organization (2011), and WHO (2015c). 47. The indicator ratio of students enrolled in health workforce education and training programs to qualified educators measures the level of human resource input in terms of the number of educators relative to the size of the student population. 48. The numerator is the total number of students enrolled in health workforce education and training programs in a given year. 49. The denominator is the total number of qualified educators for health workforce education and training programs in the same year. 50. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program. 51. The glossary includes terms such as health workforce education and training place, health workforce education and training program, qualified educators, and students. 52. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is annual. 53. Potential data sources include databases of health education and training institutions. 54. Further information and related references include UNESCO (2009), UNESCO (2017), and Pan American Health Organization (2011). 55. The indicator rate of students from a cohort exiting a health workforce education and training program without completion measures the drop-out rate. 56. The numerator is the number of students from a cohort not completing or repeating a year of a health workforce education and training program. 57. The denominator is the number of students from the same cohort who enrolled in the program the previous year. 58. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program and by sex. 59. The glossary includes terms such as drop-out, health workforce education and training program, sex, and student. 60. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is annual. 61. Potential data sources include databases of health education and training institutions. 62. Further information and related references include UNESCO (2009), UNESCO (2017), and Pan American Health Organization (2011). 63. The indicator ratio of the number of students graduating from a health workforce education and training program to the number of students enrolled in the first year of the same program measures the graduation rate. 64. The numerator is the number of graduates from a cohort of a health workforce education and training program. 65. The denominator is the number of students enrolled in the first year of the same program. 66. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program. 67. The glossary includes terms such as graduate, health workforce education and training program, sex, and student. 68. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is annual. 69. Potential data sources include databases of health education and training institutions. 70. Further information and related references include WHO (2016c) and WHO (2015a). 71. Module 3 focuses on the regulation and accreditation of education institutions. 72. It includes standards for the duration and content of education and training, accreditation mechanisms, social accountability, social determinants of health, interprofessional education, and lifelong learning. 73. The indicator existence of national and/or subnational standards on the duration and content of health workforce education and training determines whether such standards are established. 74. The numerator and denominator are not applicable for this indicator. 75. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program. 76. The glossary includes terms such as health workforce education and training program. 77. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is every three years. 78. Potential data sources include ministries of health, ministries of education, and similar institutions. 79. Further information and related references include the European Union (2013), WHO (2013e), and WFME (2015). 80. The indicator existence of national and/or subnational mechanisms for accreditation of health workforce education and training institutions and their programs determines whether such mechanisms are established and whether they are compulsory. 81. The numerator and denominator are not applicable for this indicator. 82. Disaggregation is performed by health workforce education and training program. 83. The glossary includes terms such as accreditation mechanisms. 84. Data reporting frequency for this indicator is every three years. 85. Potential data sources include ministries of health, ministries of education, national accreditation authorities, statutory corporations, and professional councils. 86. Further information and related references include WHO (2016c), WHO (2013c), and WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean (2011).
